# L31.4c Glass Curtain-Wall Response, Failure and Reliability (Exploring)

L31.4c addresses the PI's third question under L31.4 (non-Gaussian wind pressure and facades): given a wind-pressure time history, how to compute a glass curtain-wall panel's response, judge failure and assess reliability, including whether one broken panel can trigger progressive failure. The Lead agent split the work into six packages (c1 to c6): failure modes, panel net load, plate response, failure criteria, single-panel reliability and facade cascade. A full first version of the chain was built in one day, with each step pre-registered before computation. A review of six key judgments forced recalculation and voided several earlier numbers. All results are internal and preliminary. They apply to one configuration: the CAARC building, a single pressure tap standing in for each panel, a single-room zero-order quasi-steady internal pressure model and a 5 h design cyclone. They are conditional failure probabilities for that storm, not annual probabilities and not "curtain-wall failure probabilities".

## Timeline
- **2026-10-25**: Work started after the PI approved the L31.4 plan v2. With only one glass-side literature card in the knowledge base, two literature requests were sent. After the PI asked to see the packages, each package was opened as a visible conversation.
- **2026-10-25**: The c1 failure-mode list v1 (15 modes) was delivered. Mode shares could not be estimated, because no survey, including those of Chinese typhoons, gives the total number of panels inspected.
- **2026-10-25**: The c4 criteria comparison v0 treated Brown integration, the Weibull glass-strength model and ASTM E1300 as three steps of one chain, not competing criteria. The c3 plate-response note v0 used a large-deflection plate solver, but its three pre-registered validation checks failed. Whether a quasi-static analysis is adequate could not be decided from the CAARC data.
- **2026-10-25**: First c5 and c6 results reported a time-history effect of 1.3 to 1.6 times the nominal 0.008 failure probability, and a "clear" cascade.
- **2026-10-25**: Five of six requested independent reviewer reports were received, with 9 must-fix items. Three items changed numbers: resistance had been calibrated separately for each pressure side, 5 roof tap groups (16 roof taps) had been mixed into the 35 corner tap groups, and the Gaussian comparison had been applied beyond the taps where it was tested. The earlier c5 and c6 numbers were withdrawn.
- **2026-10-25**: After recalculation with one envelope-based resistance per panel, the time-history effect largely disappeared: the failure probability was 0.0084 to 0.0093 for panels designed to the 50% peak. Designing with Gaussian-estimated peaks raised failure probability 3.0 to 5.0 times, reported only for 12 strongly non-Gaussian suction-side facade tap groups (main resistance model). A south-face opening raised it 2.8 to 3.8 times for panels designed as enclosed.
- **2026-10-25**: Dynamic amplification mattered only as an upper bound: 2.6 to 4.8 times, if the panel-support frequency is about 4 Hz and the spectral slope above 1 Hz is −5/3. That frequency band may be affected by tubing artefacts in the wind-tunnel data.
- **2026-10-25**: In the cascade rerun, given at least one broken panel, the probability of at least one cascade failure was 0.24 to 0.35, judged "clear", though cascades mostly added only 1 panel. Without that condition, the probability was 0.010 to 0.020. The Lead agent wrote the corrected v1 summary.

## What the PI decided
- The PI approved the L31.4 restructuring plan v2, which serves as this sub-project's start-up plan ("OK, now you can proceed as you said").
- The PI asked to see every work package in the interface, so each package was opened as a separate conversation.

## Where it stands
The corrected first-version summary is with the L31.4 Lead. Next steps are replacing single-tap loads with panel-area averaging, firming up the dynamic term and adding dynamic or multi-room internal pressure. Whether the wind-tunnel pressure data were corrected for tubing response can only be settled by asking the data authors; that external contact was referred to the PI.

projects.title: L31.4c1 Curtain Wall Construction and Failure Modes
projects.digest:
# L31.4c1 Curtain Wall Construction and Failure Modes (Active)

This work package lists the wind-related failure modes of common curtain wall systems and asks which dominate in real typhoons and hurricanes. On 2026-10-25, after new literature cards arrived and one source was checked against the original over 4 pages, the package Lead agent delivered failure-mode list v1 ahead of its 11-01 due date, with no computation. It contains 15 modes: 3 to be modelled (wind-pressure glass breakage, outer-pane versus full-unit failure of insulating glass, laminated glass before breakage), 4 to be treated as inputs (such as impact pre-damage as a strength-reduction parameter), and 8 listed only. Investigators of two US hurricanes judged windborne debris the main cause, but the only figure (over 80% for Hurricane Alicia, from a glass dealer report) is counted as one source; no source gives the number of panels inspected, so mode shares cannot be computed. No peer-reviewed mode-by-mode survey with a denominator was found for Chinese typhoons, and reported case counts were labelled as counts, not rates.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-25**: Package opened under the plan approved by the PI.
- **2026-10-25**: List v1 (15 modes) delivered; a follow-up pass collected all case counts with their definitions.

## Where it stands
The package moves to maintenance, updating the list if later tasks find new modes. Panel failure probabilities from the reliability task apply only to undamaged, ideally supported panels failing under wind pressure, not to curtain walls as a whole. Remaining gaps include per-panel statistics and data on post-impact strength loss.

projects.title: L31.4c2 From Pressure Taps to Panel Net Load
projects.digest:
# L31.4c2 From Pressure Taps to Net Panel Loads (Active)

This work package of L31.4c (glass curtain wall response, failure and reliability) asks how tap pressures become the load on a single cladding panel: area averaging, combining external and internal pressure into net pressure, and what to do when taps are too sparse. The Lead agent found that CAARC taps are about 4.4 m apart horizontally and 9–30 m vertically at full scale (1:400), much larger than a typical 1.5 m × 3 m panel, so panel-scale averaging is not possible and one tap stands in for one panel, a conservative choice whose margin was not quantified. Version 0 produced a 5 h example net-pressure history (154 260 points) for a wall-corner tap at about 90 m, matching earlier week-4 results to a maximum relative difference of 2.4×10⁻⁹; across 300 seeds the suction damage-equivalent coefficient (s=10) spanned 4.01–4.64 (p10–p90), so downstream reliability work must use many seeds. Version 0.1 replaced internal pressure with the a5 v0 quasi-steady model and added ±0.55 constant levels. All results are internal, preliminary, unreviewed and limited to this tap, this floor, a zero-order internal-pressure model and assumed scaling (1/8 velocity scale, K_q=1).

## Timeline
- **2026-10-25**: Work-package note written; the brief's assumption of denser taps in the 1:200 model was found not to hold.
- **2026-10-25**: Version 0 delivered at zero supercomputer and Colab cost. Two preregistration items were fixed after seeing results and labelled as such: the example tap was moved from a roof tap to a wall tap, and native sampling was recommended because interpolation to 0.1 s lowered the damage-equivalent coefficient by 6–8%.
- **2026-10-25**: The parent Lead set two internal-pressure options and said not to wait for correlation lengths. Version 0.1 followed: median suction coefficients were 4.31 / 4.50 / 4.91 for constant 0 / +0.18 / +0.55; a south-face opening gave 5.74, the only case worse than +0.55 (17% higher); the sealed case gave 3.80. Sealed-case internal pressure exceeded ±0.18, but this is attributed to the unfiltered zero-order model and is not evidence that the code value is too small.
- **2026-10-25**: Some timestamps in v0 files were found to be 20–60 minutes off and corrected; the order of steps was unchanged. A startup-plan reminder was judged a false alarm for a work package.

## What the PI decided
- Approved the L31.4 plan v2, under which this work package runs.

## Where it stands
Next: add the dynamic (Helmholtz) internal-pressure version once a5 provides it, and a panel-scale reduction once b2 supplies tap correlation lengths.

projects.title: L31.4c3 Panel Structural Response
projects.digest:
# L31.4c3 Glass Panel Response (Active)

This work package of L31.4c (glass curtain wall response, failure and reliability) asks how to compute stress histories in a glass panel from net pressure: large-deflection geometric nonlinearity, whether quasi-static analysis suffices or dynamics are needed, laminated glass, and load sharing in insulating glass units. Because the existing finite-element pipeline does not support geometric nonlinearity, the Lead agent wrote its own von Kármán large-deflection finite-difference solver for simply supported rectangular panels, built stress-pressure tables for aspect ratios 1–3, and provided an interface that converts a net-pressure history into maximum principal stress histories for single, insulating and laminated panels. Three of four preregistered verification checks failed (only the linear check passed); the solver's usability rests on an after-the-fact diagnosis, an inference, not a passed verification. The local stress-pressure exponent falls as low as 0.5–0.7, giving an equivalent pressure exponent of about 8–15 that varies with panel and load level. Whether dynamics matter cannot be decided from the CAARC wind-tunnel record, because the panel's natural frequency (about 14 Hz) lies in a frequency band the data do not resolve reliably. All work used small workstation scripts only (0 SU, 0 Colab units) and is unreviewed.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-25**: Work-package note written; the Lead agent chose a four-tier approach (linear solution, E1300 curves, own large-deflection script, finite elements only if triggered).
- **2026-10-25**: Model description v0 delivered ahead of the 11-08 deadline. Corner peak stress was about 6% above the original paper on finer grids, beyond the 5% tolerance, attributed to the original's coarse grid; the criterion was not changed. Insulating-unit load sharing of 51.7%/48.3% reproduced the original 51.8%/48.2%. Laminated glass is given only as layered and fully composite bounds. Five triggers for finite-element work were listed, not commissioned.
- **2026-10-25**: A startup-plan reminder was judged a false alarm for a work package.
- **2026-10-25**: Following a review ruling, v0.1 states that checks V1 (2.1% > 2%), V2 (+6.3%/+6.1% > 5%) and V3 (+18% > 15%) failed; the 0.1% agreement applies only on the original 20×32 grid against two Vallabhan–Chou 1986 points; the high-frequency spectral anomaly's cause is unconfirmed, with tubing resonance only a guess.
- **2026-10-25**: The v0 dynamic-sensitivity method was withdrawn after a reviewer showed it could not reach the resonance frequency. A new interface extrapolates the spectrum above about 1 Hz full scale with a power law. CAARC demonstration (119 corner taps, 10 mm 1.5×3.0 m panel, 2% damping, point pressures): median peak amplification +3% (90th percentile +8%) with the fitted slope, and +15% (+19%) with a −5/3 slope.

## What the PI decided
- Approved the L31.4 plan v2, under which this work package runs.

## Where it stands
Dynamic results are sensitivity bounds only and both slopes must be reported. Deciding quasi-static versus dynamic needs to know whether the wind-tunnel data were tubing-corrected and panel-scale spectra or correlation lengths from b2.

projects.title: L31.4c4 Comparison of Glass Failure Criteria
projects.digest:
# L31.4c4 Comparison of Glass Failure Criteria (Active)

This work package of L31.4c (glass curtain wall response, failure and reliability) compares three glass failure criteria: Brown's integral for static fatigue, the surface-flaw Weibull strength model (glass failure prediction model), and the ASTM E1300 3 s equivalent load, and asks how much non-Gaussian tails and load duration add to damage. The Lead agent treated the three not as alternatives but as links in one chain (time history to equivalent constant load, to failure probability, and the E1300 simplification), with differences located at the interfaces: stress versus pressure exponent, reference duration and flaw area. Using first-hand literature cards, it derived s = nβ (n=16) and showed that the factor 1.2 used to convert a 60 s resistance to 3 s matches 20^(1/16)=1.206 from Beason and Morgan 1984; that the two share a source is an inference. Because the E1300-24 text was not obtained, two readings of its reference duration are kept side by side; this does not affect the load-side baseline but does affect failure probability. Baseline figures are internal and preliminary, valid only for this dataset and configuration (5 h design cyclone, 35 corner tracks, point pressures rather than panel averages). No new computation was run.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-25**: Work-package note and v0 draft written from secondary sources. Baseline: time-history 3 s equivalent load is 1.00–1.11 of the 50th-percentile peak and 0.84–0.94 of the 90th; non-Gaussian tails raise suction-side load by 9–24% (damage 2.3–29 times) and positive-pressure load by 2–5%; the two effects cannot simply be added.
- **2026-10-25**: Literature cards arrived; v0 was finalized ahead of the 11-01 deadline with primary sources, and a worker-facing recommendation that the c5 reliability step compute a 60 s equivalent stress directly from the stress history, with reading 1 as main value and reading 2 as sensitivity.
- **2026-10-25**: A startup-plan reminder was judged a false alarm for a work package.
- **2026-10-25**: Following a review ruling, v0.1 restated the earlier "up to 1.5–1.6 times" claim: 1.52/1.63 is a ratio of risk integrals (m=6/7, exact 20^(1/16)); with the rounded 1.2 used in c5, failure-probability ratios at the design point are 1.67 (E7), 1.74 (HZ) and 2.67 (OS) at s=10, 1.25–1.48 at s=13, and 1.03–1.04 at s=16, i.e. not zero difference.

## What the PI decided
- Approved the L31.4 plan v2, under which this work package runs.

## Where it stands
v0.1 is delivered for c5 to freeze its preregistration. The plate exponent β awaits c3; until then s=10/13/16 are used as sensitivity levels. Three papers remain placeholder cards, and E1300-24 and IABSE SED10 were not obtained.

projects.title: L31.4c5 Single-Panel Reliability
projects.digest:
# L31.4c5 Single-Panel Reliability of Glass Facades (Active)

This work package combines load uncertainty (wind speed, Cp, peak estimation, method bias) with glass resistance statistics to estimate a single facade panel's failure probability in a design storm. The result is compared with the 8/1000 probability built into the ASTM E1300 glass design method. The chain was calibrated so that a panel designed exactly to the code-style 3 s peak times E1300 has failure probability 0.008. Results then depend only on the ratio of the time-history-equivalent load to that peak and on the shape of the resistance distribution. Corner-zone tracks of the CAARC model from earlier work were used, with each single tap standing in for a panel. Every step followed a frozen preregistration or a dated supplement, ran locally with 0 SU, and has not been reviewed. After an independent review required envelope design (one design load, one resistance, failure if either face exceeds it), the median conditional failure probability was 0.0084 to 0.0093 with no load uncertainty, within twice 0.008. All values are conditional on one design storm, are not annual probabilities, and must not be called facade failure probabilities.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-25**: The Lead agent wrote the package note and a draft preregistration, with three resistance models drawn from literature cards (one marked a second-hand account of E1300) and operational definitions such as "close to 8/1000" meaning 0.004 to 0.016.
- **2026-10-25**: The preregistration was frozen at 11:36 and the full chain run (v0). With load uncertainty included, median failure probabilities were 0.023, 0.030 and 0.049 for the three response settings, judged "significantly high". However, the code-style design itself reached 0.015 to 0.035 under the same load uncertainty, which used non-hurricane placeholder values. Using a Gaussian assumption for peaks raised failure probability by 2.6 to 4.5 times.
- **2026-10-25**: v1 used 600-seed panel time histories with 17 internal-pressure cases. With internal pressure equal to its design value, medians were 0.008 to 0.011 ("close"). A south-face opening on an enclosed-design panel gave 0.023, 0.029 and 0.043, 2.8 to 3.9 times higher. The main reading was switched, after seeing v0, to "no load uncertainty"; this was disclosed and both readings were listed.
- **2026-10-25**: The review-driven rerun (v0.1/v1.1) removed roof tracks (30 facade tracks), restricted the Gaussian-peak comparison to 12 strongly non-Gaussian suction tracks (3.0 to 5.0 times), corrected a reported range from 0.22–0.37 to 0.22–0.34, and added two unverified assumptions to the caveats. For the enclosed design with a south opening, the increase was 2.78 to 3.82 times relative to constant internal pressure, 5.6 to 10.9 times relative to the enclosed quasi-steady case and 2.85 to 5.31 times relative to 0.008.
- **2026-10-25**: A dynamic-amplification sensitivity check, an upper bound only, gave ratios of 1.01 to 1.07 at typical panel frequencies (13.7 and 25 Hz) with the fitted spectral slope. Only the 4 Hz, −5/3-slope case changed most verdicts (2.57 to 4.78 times). It relies on extrapolation above 1 Hz, which the records cannot support.

## What the PI decided
- Approved the L31.4 plan v2, under which this package runs. All instructions in this conversation came from the parent Lead agent.

## Where it stands
The next steps depend on per-panel response exponents and real panel frequencies from c3, and transient internal pressure from a5. Combining these results with opening probabilities is outside this package. Any claim such as "an opening raises failure probability several-fold" must go to independent review first.

projects.title: L31.4c6 Progressive Facade Failure
projects.digest:
# L31.4c6 Progressive Failure of Glass Facades (Active)

This work package asks whether breaking one glass panel, by changing the internal pressure, raises net pressures on other panels enough to cause cascading failures. It also asks how many further failures a debris-made opening triggers, and how to compute facade-level failure probability and expected damage. Post-storm surveys give examples both for and against cascades. The Lead agent therefore designed a paired counterfactual. The same resistance samples and the same 5 h design storm are run twice, once with internal pressure updated as openings form (pass A) and once with it frozen at the sealed state (pass B). A panel that fails in A but not in B counts as a cascade. Two runs (0 SU locally, then one CRC Python job) both met the preregistered "cascade evident" verdict. Conditional probabilities were about 0.24 to 0.36, and the unconditional probability of at least one cascading panel was low. All results are internal and preliminary, have not been reviewed, and are conditional on one design storm in one configuration. They are not annual facade failure probabilities.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-25**: The work package note was written, with no computation. Its start conditions were a single-panel example, an internal-pressure model v0 and the panel layout convention.
- **2026-10-25**: The parent Lead gave the start order for a minimal test using 32 taps on one floor of the CAARC model, each standing for one panel, with 6 storm directions and 20 realizations. The preregistration was frozen at 12:29. Two documented implementation changes followed (a faster exact pressure solver, and fewer capacity samples per storm), with the criteria unchanged.
- **2026-10-25**: Run c6-01 gave P(at least one cascade | at least one failure) of 0.3198, 0.3253 and 0.3621 for the three resistance settings. Cascades were mostly one panel, and the failure-count amplification was 1.28 to 1.43. All four forced-opening debris scenarios were "evident". The Lead agent noted that counting any break as an opening, one tap per panel, and a single room may all overestimate cascades.
- **2026-10-25**: After an independent review, the parent Lead ordered a rerun in which each panel is designed for the larger of its positive and suction design loads, plus revised aggregation and added caveats. A post-review addendum was frozen before the run, and an addendum on a self-check lower bound was written after a smoke test but before the main run.
- **2026-10-25**: Run c6-03 gave direction-equal-weight conditional probabilities of 0.2531, 0.2390 and 0.2683 and weighted values of 0.2830, 0.2993 and 0.3548, all "cascade evident". Unconditional probabilities were 0.0204, 0.0128 and 0.0103. A windward forced opening stayed "evident" (0.3714 and 0.3473), but a leeward opening dropped to "no verdict" (0.0914 and 0.0837). One self-check failed under the original wording and passed under the addendum; both readings were reported. The earlier way of computing unconditional probability was withdrawn.

## What the PI decided
- Approved the L31.4 plan v2, under which this package runs. All other instructions in this conversation came from the parent Lead agent.

## Where it stands
The c6-03 results are with the parent Lead. Two assumptions remain unverified: that the code internal-pressure coefficient and this line's Cp share the same reference dynamic pressure, and that the whole chain is quasi-static. The proposed next steps are to count an opening only when both glass layers fail, to add a multi-room internal pressure model, and to replace single taps with area-averaged loads. Any "cascade evident" conclusion must be reviewed before it goes to the PI.

# L31.5 抗风设计规范与设计原则的演进（课题 5）

## 开题卡（10-16 v1，未做研究）
**核心科学问题**：几十年来抗风规范（ASCE 7 及其前身、GB 50009、EN 1991-1-4、AIJ）在设计原则上发生过哪些根本转变？例如：容许应力到分项系数；重现期加荷载系数到直接用长重现期风速；平均风速到阵风风速；风速图从统计到台风模拟；风向系数；性能化抗风；新增龙卷荷载。每次转变的驱动力是什么（灾害教训、新数据、可靠度标定、方法进步）？对同一座结构，设计荷载究竟变了多少？变化来自危险性、荷载模型还是可靠度目标？由此能否判断下一步该往哪里演进？

**现有认识与空白**
- 库内有：国际主要规范顺风向荷载效应比较（Zhou、Kijewski、Kareem 2002） p.1–5，风速链 `V=V0*Cdirection*...` 见 Eq.(6)，200 m 算例见 p.3–5；ASCE 7-22 风荷载接口精读（含龙卷荷载 W_T） p.1–7（PDF p.62–68）；气候变化对美国极端风暴与结构设计的影响。
- 10-16 补卡（litwiki，前缀）。
 - 可靠度标定：Ellingwood、Galambos、MacGregor、Cornell 1980，NBS SP577，为 ANSI A58 提出概率极限状态荷载系数 `XGR8CMFK_*`（PDF p.9 = 印刷 p.1）。
 - 规范化方法：Simiu & Stathopoulos 1997 用钝体空气动力学和气候数据库做规范化 `F2V8D9HM_*`；Guo 等 2025 ASCE 7 统一气动系数方法 `R55AM6K9_*`。
 - 荷载链：Isyumov 2012 Davenport 的贡献（风荷载链）`GZDPJ9AF_*`；Kareem、Hu、Guo、Kwon 2019 广义风荷载链 `3R5RN3GT_*`；Hangan 等 2019 三维、非平稳、非高斯风场及其对风–结构问题的影响 `CVDCDIRU_*`；Kareem 2020 风工程前沿 `W2H28A3F_*`。
 - 性能化：ASCE 2019 性能化抗风设计预标准 `PPHBMPDP_*`。
- 空白：GB 50009（2001/2012）和 EN 1991-1-4 没有可核的合法全文；Mehta 的 ASCE 7 风荷载条文史原文未核实；平台上 ASCE 7 只有 7-16 和 7-22。初判（待核实）：已有文献多是"同时期跨国"的横向比较或单一方法论，"同一规范跨版本"的纵向分解（危险性、荷载模型、系数/可靠度）很少。

**切入点与可用数据/工具**（只读引用）
- ASCE 7-16 和 7-22 原文及接口图：、。
- ASCE 与中国规范适用性说明（只有计划）：。
- 更好世界 T1（结构非线性）和 T3（性能化/韧性）有关于设计原则的论述框架，只读互引。

**第一步最小实验**（0 SU，文档工作）
- (a) 演进时间轴和"设计原则转变"矩阵：版本 × 原则维度，包括可靠度格式、重现期、风速定义、风速图来源、风向、暴露、阵风效应、性能化、龙卷。每格引用条文和页码，取不到原文的标"缺"。
- (b) 纵向分解算例：一座 CAARC 型高层和一座低矮房屋，在同一场地分别按 ASCE 7 各可得版本计算设计风荷载，把变化分解为危险性、荷载模型和系数/可靠度三部分。
- 判据：如果分解显示某次版本变化的主要驱动不是危险性，而是格式或系数，就说明"规范演进的驱动"值得系统研究。然后把同样的分解扩到 GB 50009 和 EN。

**预计工作量**：约 8–10 人-日、0 SU。主要瓶颈是旧版规范原文，需由 Liang Hu 或图书馆提供；先列缺失版本清单。

# L31.5a Shared Load-Chain Steps (Not started)

This node of L31.5 (evolution of wind-resistant design codes) handles the load-chain steps common to all structure types, so that the other nodes (b to f) can use its edition-to-edition ratios. The start-up plan, written by the parent coordinator, awaits the PI's approval. The Lead agent confirmed that the ASCE 7-02, 7-05, 7-10, 7-16 and 7-22 texts, AASHTO 2004/05 and all 13 literature cards listed in the plan are available. It added two method points for the task briefs: for the 7-05 to 7-10 change, wind speed maps and load factors must be evaluated together, because 7-10 replaced "50-year wind speed × 1.6W" with "700-year wind speed × 1.0W", so a joint C1×C6 ratio will be given and the separate ratios flagged as not interpretable alone; and the node covers only steps C1, C2, C3 and C6, so their product is not the total load ratio, which can close only after the structure nodes supply C4 (aerodynamic) and C5 (dynamic). No results yet.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: Node created at the PI's request; read-only checks completed and three second-level sub-projects proposed: a1 wind climate and wind speed maps, a2 site and direction, a3 design format and reliability.

## Where it stands
Awaiting approval of the start-up plan. Planned: a 7-02/7-05/7-10 clause comparison table in week 1 and a per-step ratio table v1 for two sites in week 2.

This node of L31.5 (evolution of wind-resistant design codes) covers wind provisions for other structures: signs, solid walls, rooftop equipment, ground-mounted solar panels, chimneys, water tanks and lattice towers. # L31.5e Bridges (Not started)

This node of L31.5 (evolution of wind-resistant design codes) traces how wind provisions for bridges in AASHTO LRFD changed across editions. The start-up plan was written by the parent coordinator and awaits the PI's approval; the Lead agent only read the plan and four literature cards (an NCHRP wind load revision report, Nieto 2010 on short-span bridge code comparison, Scanlan 1981 on flutter, vortex shedding and buffeting, and Mehrabi 2007 on stay cable vibration). Three of these cards state that the source does not say which AASHTO edition adopted the changes, so the near-term deliverable can only be edition changes as recounted in the literature, not an established basis for each revision. The Lead agent found two scope corrections for the static wind subtask: construction-stage wind loads are not in Section 3.8.1 of the 2004/05 edition but come from later proposals and a 2017 guide, and the plan omitted Section 3.8.2 (vertical wind pressure); whether the 2004 edition contains 3.8.2 has not yet been checked. No results yet.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: Node created at the PI's request; read-only review completed and two second-level sub-projects proposed: L31.5e1 static wind loads (3.8.1, with 3.8.2) and L31.5e2 wind-induced vibration and aeroelastic stability (3.8.3).

## Where it stands
Awaiting approval of the start-up plan. First steps after approval: open e1 and e2, build the project page, and locate Section 3.8 in the 2004/05 scan.

projects.title: L31.6 Probabilistic methods in wind engineering
projects.report:
# 6c 评判清单："一个概率/随机方法对风工程有没有用"（v1.1，10-17）
核心实验室起草，更好世界实验室共用（只读引用）。本实验室是公开项目（Liang Hu 10-17 全部撤销不公开）。
- v0（10-16）：10 条，其中 1–5 落地侧由本实验室起草，6–10 批判侧由更好世界给出。
- v1.2（10-18）：第 4 条加一句"重现期越长不确定带越宽，需按重现期分别写带宽"（更好世界 L29.5 对表）。
- v1.1（10-17）：更好世界对表后改三处：第 12 条门槛标"本线约定"并补等效样本量；第 4 条区分两种"没超过不确定带"；写明 6–10 条哪些算否决。新增 0、11、12 条两边都采用，第 11 条改为"共用"。
- v1（10-17）：用 L31.6 第一个试金石（台风危险性去聚合）试用后修订。改动见文末「v0→v1 改动」。10 条的原意不变，6–10 条措辞未改。

## 怎么用
每个方法族逐条打分，四档：**过 / 条件过（写条件）/ 不过 / 未评（写缺什么证据）**。每条附证据：卡片与页码、本线数据路径，或"无文献依据，基于本线数据"。一个方法族一行，汇总在方法地图。

| # | 条目 | 侧 | 判"过"的最低要求 | 证据形式 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 方法定义能否复现 | 共用（v1 新增） | 输入、输出、关键假设写得出来，能和同族方法区分开 | 原文式号或页码 |
| 1 | 问题是否真实 | 落地 | 对应风工程里一个具体的设计或评估问题，写出规范条文或评估环节 | 条文号或环节名 |
| 2 | 比现行做法强在哪 | 落地 | 写明现行做法，说清增益属于哪类：精度、效率、能回答新问题 | 现行做法出处 |
| 3 | 风工程数据上能否复现 | 落地 | 在至少一组实测、风洞或已有模拟数据上复现出增益 | 数据路径和结果文件 |
| 4 | 对设计结论是否有可见影响 | 落地 | 设计荷载、构件选择或失效概率的变化超过既有不确定带。不确定带要写出数值，例如 bootstrap 区间。**区分两种"没超过"**：影响确实小于一个合理宽度的带，记"不过"；带本身宽到任何方法都超不过（如每站只有 14 场风暴），记"未评（样本不足）"，不记"不过" **重现期越长不确定带越宽，需按重现期分别写带宽**（L29.5 真值试验 10-18：重复间 RMSE 50/700/1700 年约 6–7%/11–12%/13–15%，见）。 | 数值和区间 |
| 5 | 数据与计算是否可得 | 落地 | 工程中拿得到所需输入，计算成本在设计周期内可接受 | 输入清单和耗时 |
| 6 | 与已有方法是否实质等价 | 批判（29） | 去掉等价部分后仍有独立增益 | — |
| 7 | 证据能否复核 | 批判（29） | 数据、代码或参数公开，或可由我们复算 | — |
| 8 | 增益是否超过输入假设本身的不确定性，且不是因为输入假设不同造成的 | 批判（29） | 在同一输入假设下比较，增益仍大于输入不确定性 | — |
| 9 | 是否在统一基准上比较 | 批判（29） | 同数据、同指标、同计算预算 | — |
| 10 | 优势出现在什么条件下，能否事先说明 | 批判（29） | 能事先写出适用条件，不是事后挑出来的 | — |
| 11 | 移植时风灾特有的物理差异是否处理了 | 共用（v1 新增；6b、3d 必查，6a 的非平稳算例也查） | 逐项说明以下四点在方法里怎么处理，或为什么无关（优化算法、代理模型等与风灾物理无关的方法族，写"无关"并附一句理由）：**持续时间**（风暴持续数小时，地震持续数十秒）；**非平稳**；**方向性**（风向与结构主轴）；**混合风气候**（台风、雷暴、温带系统） | 逐项一句 |
| 12 | 尾部有多少样本支撑 | 共用（v1 新增） | 写出决定结论的事件数；没有事件可数的方法（如峰值估计）写等效样本量（如独立分段数）。设计重现期附近少于约 30 个时，结论只能写"条件过"，并给出样本不确定性。**"约 30"是本线约定，无文献依据** | 事件数或等效样本量，和区间 |

## 判定
- **有用**：0–5 和 11 全过，6–10 没有否决项，12 过。
- **6–10 条的否决项**：第 6 条不过（与已有方法完全等价）或第 8 条不过（增益来自输入假设不同），不能判"有用"，最多"有条件有用"。第 7、9、10 条不过，该条降为"条件过"并写明条件。
- **有条件有用**：部分条目只在特定条件下过。写明条件；12 不过的，一律只能到这一档。
- **无用**：第 1 条或第 4 条"不过"（第 4 条"未评（样本不足）"不算）；或者第 11 条有一项会改变结论但无法处理。
- **未评**：第 3、4 条证据还没有。方法地图里大多数方法族目前都在这一档，这是正常的。
- 判为无用的名单交更好世界，到对方只算候选（分工约定 a）。两边预判相反时，按约定 b 用同一试金石、同一份清单，一方计算、另一方复核。

## v1→v1.1 改动（10-17，更好世界对表）
1. 第 12 条：门槛"约 30"标为本线约定，无文献依据；补"等效样本量"。
2. 第 4 条与判定：区分"不过"与"未评（样本不足）"。
3. 判定：写明否决项（第 6、8 条）与降档项（第 7、9、10 条）。
4. 第 11 条"侧"改为"共用"，并写明无关方法族的处理。
5. 更好世界的 T5 判据（分位差 ≥5% 或排序改变）不改，与第 4 条并列报告，两种口径都报。

## v0→v1 改动（10-17）
1. **新增第 0 条**。PEM 题名初分时发现两个问题：
 - 一篇常同时属于几族，例如第 62 篇既是易损性，又是多保真代理
 - 题名含 wind 的 62 篇里有 9 篇是风能、4 篇是其他领域（摘要核对后）；另有 6 篇按题名分错族，读摘要才改对。
 所以先要说清"方法是什么、解决哪个问题"，再谈有没有用。
2. **新增第 11 条**。去聚合试金石第一步只能回答"哪类风暴主导设计风速"；开题卡判据的后半句（持续时间、风向是否与规范的隐含假设不同）必须另算。地震方法搬到风上，最容易漏的就是这四类差异。v0 只在开题卡正文里提了一句，没有进清单。
3. **新增第 12 条**。STORM 1 万年目录在每个站点上，超过 V700 的只有 14 场风暴。去聚合结论建立在 14 个事件上，必须把样本量写出来。条件均值类方法也有同样的问题：Baker 2011 指出，只匹配条件均值谱会低估响应离散性，所引研究低估峰值位移标准差 30%–50%（卡，作者稿 PDF 第 10–11 页）。
4. **第 4 条**加了一句：不确定带要写出数值。
5. **新增"怎么用"一节**：四档打分，每条附证据。
6. **判定规则**相应修订，并新增"未评"档。

# L31.6 Probabilistic Methods Applied to Wind Engineering (Exploring)

This project evaluates which probabilistic, earthquake, and coastal engineering methods add value for wind engineering under a 13-item checklist (v1.1). After five exploratory testbeds, the Lead agent expanded the survey per the PI's instructions to 34,950 papers across 15 method journals versus 8,116 wind papers, mapping 144 methods in 14 families. In the unreviewed testbeds, hazard deaggregation and the joint probability method had prior hurricane precedents (Dong et al. (2022); Sheng & Hong (2020); Vickery & Blanton (2008)), with deaggregation across 3 stations failing duration (-7% to -14%, intervals spanning 0) and direction (within 10 percentage points) criteria (0/3 stations). Probability-box bounds across 12 inland stations gave a median 700-year wind width of 10.44 m/s, with the upper bound exceeding Gumbel by more than 5% at only 1/12 stations (no visible effect on design values) with pressure bounds undecidable, while spectral record selection failed in stationary wind-tunnel data (1 building, 1 direction, 6 segments) and across 28 measured thunderstorms (0/3 periods passing both yield levels). Only inter-event/intra-event decomposition of ASOS 5 s / 2 min gust factors passed for typhoons (32 storms, 37 stations: inter-event share 0.28; two-site joint exceedance 1.87 times independence), rated conditionally useful only for multi-site risk pending sensor-change and Sheng et al. (2024) full-text checks. Cross-checking 79 methods with independent reviewer models left 16 blank structural wind-engineering methods and 14 sub-projects (L31.6a to L31.6n).

## Timeline
- **2026-10-16**: Following PI approval, the Lead agent started L31.6 to refine the checklist, classify 62 *Probabilistic Engineering Mechanics* papers, and design a 0 SU deaggregation testbed.
- **2026-10-17**: Finalized checklist v1.1, grouped the 62 papers into 11 families, and ran the deaggregation testbed (19 stations in step one, 3 in step two), finding prior precedents and 0/3 stations passing duration or direction criteria.
- **2026-10-19**: After the PI noted that other sub-projects were unrelated and L31.6 was too narrow, the agent expanded journal screening and ran four more testbeds before pausing for replanning.
- **2026-10-22**: The PI halted external bulk literature downloading and citation snowballing.
- **2026-10-25**: Directed by the PI to expand the method literature first, the Lead agent built Literature Atlas v1 (34,950 papers, 144 methods), flagging 36 methods with at most 1 wind paper and 43 with sparse usage.
- **2026-10-26**: After verifying all 79 methods with independent reviewer models and revisiting set-aside topics, the Lead agent launched L31.6a to L31.6l, voided an unphysical thunderstorm ductility clue, and submitted 12 startup plans.

## What the PI decided
- Approved basic work (2026-10-16), paused unapproved work for replanning (2026-10-19), and halted bulk literature downloading (2026-10-22).
- Clarified that other sub-projects were unrelated to L31.6, noted the scope was too narrow, and recommended adding *Earthquake Engineering & Structural Dynamics*.
- Ruled that initial testbeds were too narrow and off-target, instructing the agent to first expand the method literature, read papers, brainstorm, and form feasible topics.
- Directed the agent to verify whether the 36 and 43 methods already had wind usage, revisit set-aside topics, place all 14 topics under L31.6, promote L31.6 to a Lead, and enable periodic updates.

## Where it stands
Twelve sub-projects (L31.6a to L31.6l) await PI approval of their startup plans before computation begins, while earlier testbed results remain unreviewed internal findings. Creating L31.6m and L31.6n, transferring L31.6 to an independent Lead with monthly topic updates, and finishing full-text precedent checks await platform deployment and literature verification.

projects.title: L31.6a Non-Ergodic Typhoon Hazard
projects.digest:
# L31.6a Non-Ergodic Typhoon Wind Hazard (Not started)

This sub-project, named by the PI on 10-26 under L31.6 (bringing probabilistic methods into wind engineering), borrows the "single-station sigma" idea from earthquake engineering. Current hurricane hazard models treat the difference between modelled and observed wind as a random error per storm (Vickery et al. 2009: mean 1, CoV 10%), without distinguishing stations; if a station is biased the same way in every storm, that part is correctable, and treating it as random may inflate single-site uncertainty. The Lead agent wrote a startup plan with three criteria fixed before any computation (thresholds are the line's own assumptions, without literature basis): station terms estimated from odd and even years correlate at 0.5 or more; out-of-sample single-station sigma is at least 20% smaller; and both survive after removing the Masters et al. 2010 station-by-direction exposure correction. Fewer than 15 qualifying stations means "not evaluated", not "fail". Precedent searches (a quick search, a web search replacing Deep Research, which failed to start, and a 1,153-record citation snowball) found no study of the same question for typhoons, though site-specific bias correction is established in weather-forecast post-processing, so the claimed novelty was narrowed. No computation has been run; the plan awaits the PI's approval.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project. The plan was written: 2-minute mean wind as the main variable (avoiding a gust-definition problem between sensor types), storm-center distance over radius of maximum wind added to the baseline, public 1-minute ASOS data, no supercomputer, at most 3 Colab compute units, about 2 weeks.
- **2026-10-26**: Six "unfound" DOIs in the quick-search check were traced to stray formatting and confirmed to exist.
- **2026-10-26**: The web search showed per-station bias intercepts are mature in forecast post-processing; several of its citations had wrong DOIs or journals and were corrected or dropped.
- **2026-10-26**: Eight literature cards arrived. The Lead agent read Mohammadi et al. 2026 itself and confirmed it splits residuals into between-storm and within-storm parts with no fixed cross-storm station term. Earthquake literature gave no firm number for how much single-station sigma should shrink (one secondary figure of about 40% for earthquake sigma), so the 20% threshold stays an assumption.

## What the PI decided
- Named the sub-project; until the plan is approved only literature work and plan writing are allowed.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI's approval: the Lead agent recommends approving the whole plan, or alternatively only the precedent write-up and a data probe (at most 0.3 Colab compute units) to check whether enough stations qualify.

projects.title: L31.6b Sufficiency of Nonstationary Wind Intensity Measures
projects.digest:
# L31.6b Sufficiency of Intensity Measures for Non-Stationary Wind (Not started)

This sub-project, named by the PI on 10-26 under L31.6, tests a default assumption of performance-based wind design: that mean wind speed is a sufficient intensity measure, so that once it is fixed, strong-wind duration, rise rate and turbulence no longer affect structural response. The startup plan proposes testing this with 28 recorded thunderstorm events and comparing candidate intensity measures for efficiency, with all verdict terms defined in advance, one pre-specified main combination (peak ductility, 5% damping, yield above the mean load), at least 3 of 5 periods needed for "not sufficient", a stationary synthetic control that must come out "sufficient", and a power check: if the 28 events can detect only large effects, the result is reported as "insufficient resolution", not "sufficient". The Lead agent withdrew an earlier motivating claim (46–70% higher nonlinear demand from recorded storms) because that test had yield below the mean load and ductility values ran out of control. Precedent searches found no formal efficiency and sufficiency test of wind intensity measures; the closest prior work, Chen and Cheng 2025, already argued that peak mean wind alone is not enough, so the claimed novelty was narrowed. No computation has been run; the plan awaits approval.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project; the plan was submitted (0 SU, at most 1.5 Colab compute units, about 2 weeks, data already on the platform).
- **2026-10-26**: A quick search and a 2,415-record snowball found no same-topic work; Chen and Cheng 2025 was read and its storm intensity measure added as a sixth candidate before approval. A quick-search claim that Solari and De Gaetano 2018 did nonlinear analysis was rejected after reading the original.
- **2026-10-26**: Earthquake-engineering method cards were checked; a 10% effect-size threshold and a multiple-testing correction were added, plus a rule to test scaling bias if records are ever scaled.
- **2026-10-26**: A web search (replacing Deep Research, which failed to start) agreed with the earlier searches; two wrong DOIs and a wrong record count in it were rejected.
- **2026-10-26**: Arunachalam and Spence 2025 was carded: large per-storm differences between non-stationary and equivalent stationary loads (e.g. 74 versus 104 yielded members) but nearly equal overall collapse results (median 62.3 versus 61.8 m/s), with duration and direction changing together. Not the same question. Xu and Spence 2025 remains "not checked".

## What the PI decided
- Named the sub-project; before approval only literature work and plan writing are allowed.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI's approval of the plan, and a decision on later extending to the typhoon landfall phase, which the Lead agent suggests making after the thunderstorm results.

projects.title: L31.6c Rare-Event Sampling Inside Turbulence Simulations for Extreme Wind Pressures
projects.digest:
# L31.6c Rare-Event Sampling inside Turbulence Simulations for Extreme Wind Pressures (Not started)

This sub-project proposes to use cloning and splitting rare-event algorithms inside CFD/LBM turbulence simulations to sample the tail of short-duration peak pressures on building surfaces. The pre-set criterion for "effective" is at least a 10-fold variance reduction at equal cost, without bias, against long direct runs of the same model. The PI named it on 2026-10-26; before plan approval only literature work was done. The closest precedent, Lestang, Bouchet and Lévêque (2020), already used rare-event algorithms in a two-dimensional LBM square-cylinder flow: one algorithm (AMS) gave no gain for instantaneous drag, while another (GKTL) cut the cost of sampling extreme time-averaged drag by about 100 times. A quick literature search, a check of that paper's 20 citing works and an 817-item citation snowball found no wind engineering study that applies cloning or splitting inside a turbulence simulation for peak pressures. The claimed novelty therefore narrowed to local 1–3 s peak pressures on three-dimensional buildings in an atmospheric boundary layer, re-sampling the future inflow at each clone, and judging results by wind engineering return periods against extrapolation methods.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project; a two-phase start-up plan was written (phase 1: 2 weeks, 0 SU, at most 11 Colab compute units; phase 2: a three-dimensional Silsoe cube, estimated 35–160 GPU-hours).
- **2026-10-26**: The quick search was checked; its claim that rare-event algorithms had never been combined with LBM was rejected, since the precedent itself used LBM.
- **2026-10-26**: 11 literature cards checked; the Lead agent decided to skip a second Deep Research round because three search routes agreed.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI's approval of phase 1 and a decision on whether to proceed with the narrowed novelty (the Lead agent recommends yes); no computation will start before approval.

projects.title: L31.6d Design-Point Excitation Wind Load Time Histories
projects.digest:
# L31.6d Design-Point Excitation Wind Load Time Histories (Not started)

This sub-project asks whether two methods from earthquake engineering, the design-point excitation and the tail-equivalent linearization method (TELM), can be carried over to wind-excited nonlinear structures. The Lead agent wrote a startup plan with two testable aims: estimate exceedance probabilities of order 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁵ within 30% error at less than 1/10 the cost of subset simulation, and produce a "most likely damaging" wind load time history that adds real information beyond existing linear equivalent static wind load methods. Precision, cost and "non-equivalence" criteria were fixed before any computation; non-equivalence is a veto, and the thresholds are the line's own assumptions without literature basis. A citation snowball (1,815 records), a quick precedent search and 15 literature cards found no prior TELM or design-point work on wind-excited structures, but this rests on titles, abstracts and cards, not full reading. The original load-response-correlation (LRC) papers could not be retrieved, so the LRC comparison will be constructed by the line itself. No computation has been run; the plan awaits approval.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project; the Lead agent ran a precedent search and snowball and submitted the startup plan.
- **2026-10-26**: After the precedent report, the veto criterion was tightened to also require difference from a nonlinear LRC-style load shape, fixed before any data.
- **2026-10-26**: 13 literature cards arrived; the Lead agent read one source paper and confirmed TELM examples cover earthquake, white noise and waves only.
- **2026-10-26**: The two 1992 LRC papers were not obtained; retrieval was wrongly blocked and reported for repair.

## What the PI decided
- Named the sub-project; before plan approval only literature work and plan writing are allowed.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI's decision on starting step 1 (single-degree-of-freedom elastoplastic and Bouc-Wen systems, analytic spectra, at most 2 Colab compute units), on using analytic spectra only, and on the veto criterion.

projects.title: L31.6e Hierarchical Bayesian Wind Pressure Coefficient Database
projects.digest:
# L31.6e Hierarchical Bayesian Wind Pressure Coefficient Library (Not started)

L31.6e asks whether a hierarchical Bayesian model trained on the TPU low-rise wind-tunnel database (116 building shapes, 7 wind directions each) can predict negative peak roof pressure coefficients (corner, edge and interior zones) for shapes it has not seen. Each prediction would carry a 90% uncertainty band. Two things would be tested: whether the band really covers about 90% of held-out shapes, and whether it widens as shapes move further from the database. The motivation is that, in a cited earlier study, machine-learning pressure predictions with nominal 95% intervals covered only 56 to 64%. The PI named the sub-project on 2026-10-26, but its start-up plan has not been approved, so the Lead agent only searched the literature and wrote the plan. No pressure data were read and no computation was started. Searches with two quick web tools and three batches of literature cards (16 in total) found no study that predicts pressure coefficients for held-out shapes with interval coverage checked. These searches mostly read abstracts and are leads, not proof that the gap exists. The plan budgets about two weeks, no more than 1 TACC SU and no more than 3 Colab compute units.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project. The Lead agent wrote the start-up plan, with its decision criteria and the rule for combining them fixed before any data were seen. The thresholds are this line's own conventions, marked as assumptions.
- **2026-10-26**: The Lead agent's decisions: drop "20% lower error than the code table" as a criterion, because code values are deliberately conservative bounds and not predictions, so they are now only reported; and add conformal prediction as the strongest competitor, with "no gain" declared if it is equally calibrated and its band is no wider.
- **2026-10-26**: The quick literature search found a near neighbor that applied hierarchical Bayes to wind load variables to calibrate code factors, which narrows the novelty claim. The deeper search tool returned an error and did not run; a web search was used instead.
- **2026-10-26**: Full-text cards showed a peak-estimate sampling COV of up to 4.48 to 9.18% for 100 s model records and 12.45 to 20.01% for 10 s records. The Lead agent inferred, without computing it, that TPU's roughly 18 s records give per-tap sampling error of order 10%. The Lead agent read this as support for the plan's existing choice to model sampling error explicitly, and for its main listed risk: corner-zone noise.
- **2026-10-26**: The Lead agent added a sensitivity run with 15 peak segments (criteria still use 10). It adopted height-based roof zoning and a minimum of 4 taps for area averaging from a code-revision reanalysis, but not conversion to 1-hour peaks. A 2018 study using one pooled factor (mean 0.98, COV 0.23) was noted as a direct precedent for a later step.
- **2026-10-26**: The parent Lead decided that L31.6e and L31.6j will share one read-only TPU extraction and one peak definition, run once by L31.6e.

## What the PI decided
- Named the sub-project. This counts as agreement to set it up, not approval of the plan.

## Where it stands
The plan awaits the PI's approval. The plan suggests a first phase covering only negative roof peaks. Still open are a full-text check of a 2016 thesis (if it already predicts across shapes, this topic becomes a re-check), the deep literature search and citation snowballing.

projects.title: L31.6f Value of Information for Wind Engineering Data Investments
projects.digest:
# L31.6f Value of Information for Wind Engineering Data Investment (Not started)

This sub-project asks whether pre-posterior value-of-information analysis can decide when extra data is worth paying for in wind engineering, for example measuring wind at a site for more years, running wind tunnel tests longer, or running more CFD seeds. The PI named it on 2026-10-26; under the gate rules, only literature work and a start-up plan were allowed before plan approval, and no computation was run. The proposed first step uses 12 long-record NIST stations (32–50 years), truncates them to 5–20 years, computes the net benefit of one more year of data and checks it retrospectively against the real later years, at 0 SU, no more than 1 Colab compute unit and about 2 weeks. A literature check found that De León and Esteva (2016) already valued adding hurricane wind records for a substation and a bridge in Mexico, so the work cannot be called a first. That study compared costs after obtaining the data, at a single site, without break-even ranges by record length or retrospective tests, which the plan now names as its increment. Duthinh et al. (2018) suggest that longer wind tunnel records gain little (10 s versus 100 s differed by about 5%), so that strand was moved last.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project; the start-up plan was written and reported.
- **2026-10-26**: A quick literature search and 7 new literature cards identified the closest precedent.
- **2026-10-26**: Before touching any data, failure-cost ratio tiers were changed from 10/100/1000 to 3/30/300, bracketed by values used in two sources.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI's approval of the plan, whether to start with the record-length step only (recommended), and how to set the cost model. An earlier conference version of the precedent was still not obtained.

projects.title: L31.6g Global Sensitivity Analysis of Typhoon Wind Field Models
projects.digest:
# L31.6g Global Sensitivity of a Typhoon Wind Field Model (Exploring)

The sub-project was named by the PI on 2026-10-26 under L31.6, and is limited to literature and planning until its start-up plan is approved. While writing the plan, the Lead agent found that the original question overlaps L29.6b, which reports path sets as the largest source of difference (about 15% in Miami 100-year wind speed) and wind-field profiles at about 5%. It proposed narrowing the topic to a variance decomposition inside a typhoon boundary-layer model, separating storm parameters, boundary-layer physics schemes and sea-land roughness transition, using the PI's existing doctoral parameter sweeps (9450 storm-parameter cases, 5760 roughness-transition runs). Criteria were fixed before any computation, including a data gate of reproducing at least 3 published benchmark values; the 5% visibility threshold is a line convention with no literature basis. A quick precedent search found no study on the same question; its three nearest papers are leads not yet checked against the originals.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: Sub-project opened; the Lead agent wrote the start-up plan with pre-set criteria C1 to C3.
- **2026-10-26**: Quick precedent search returned; 5 of 6 DOIs resolved, one malformed. The follow-up Deep Research step failed with HTTP 402.

## What the PI decided
- Named the sub-project; this counts as consent to open it, not plan approval.

## Where it stands
The plan awaits the PI on four items: narrowing the topic, read-only use of the doctoral sweep data, publication handling, and division of work with L29.6b. No computation has started.

projects.title: L31.6h Shock-Degradation Service Life and Inspection of Building Envelopes
projects.digest:
# L31.6h Shock-Degradation Life and Inspection of Building Envelopes (Not started)

This sub-project, named by the PI on 10-26 under L31.6, asks whether a shock-degradation competing-failure model, in which slow deterioration such as corrosion competes with typhoons that both add damage and can cause direct failure, changes the 50-year failure probability and the optimal inspection strategy for envelope components enough to matter in practice, compared with two common simplifications (no degradation; degradation with typhoons treated as load only). The Lead agent wrote a startup plan with two pre-fixed criteria: a life criterion (50-year failure-probability ratio against the no-degradation model of 2 or more, or 0.5 or less, with at least 80% of sensitivity combinations on the same side) and an inspection criterion (the optimal strategy at least 10% cheaper in life-cycle cost than the next best, or the strategy chosen with a simplified model at least 10% more expensive under the competing-failure model); each counts as met only if at least two of three sites (Galveston, Miami, Charleston) satisfy it. All thresholds are the line's own assumptions without literature basis. Precedent checks progressively narrowed the novelty for metal roofs: Bai et al. 2023 (abstract only) already treats typhoon-induced screw fatigue with time-dependent reliability, and Mishra et al. 2019 (wood roof-to-wall connections) covers gradual degradation plus retrofit timing. The remaining candidate novelty is per-storm damage competing with atmospheric corrosion, inspection under incomplete damage information, and multi-storm life, but this cannot be confirmed without the Bai 2023 full text. No computation has been run; the plan awaits approval.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project. The plan proposed a two-week first phase at 0 SU and at most 2 Colab CPU compute units, starting with metal roof screw connections at Miami; existing synthetic typhoon data and storm-duration results would be reused.
- **2026-10-26**: A quick precedent search found Bai et al. 2023; the Lead agent shifted the metal-roof focus from life estimation to inspection decisions and corrosion-fatigue competition, keeping thresholds unchanged. Deep Research failed to start.
- **2026-10-26**: Thirteen literature cards (9 with full text) arrived; Mishra 2019 became a comparison baseline, and fatigue and cycle-rate parameters were added with page references. Coastal corrosion rates for galvanized steel are still missing, so results may end up "not evaluated (parameters uncertain)".
- **2026-10-26**: Three more cards came back without full text. The Lead agent decided that, until Bai 2023 is read, metal-roof work stops at the data probe and parameter table.

## What the PI decided
- Named the sub-project; before approval only literature work and plan writing are allowed.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI on: approving the plan; requesting Bai 2023 through interlibrary loan; doing metal roofs first (curtain-wall glass overlaps L31.4 and needs coordination); and deferring the question of field inspection data until after the first step.

projects.title: L31.6i Multi-Metric Hazard-Consistent Typhoon Subsets
projects.digest:
# L31.6i Hazard-Consistent Typhoon Subsets Matching Multiple Metrics (Not started)

This sub-project proposes to select 10–20 weighted storms per site from the STORM synthetic typhoon catalogue for Galveston, Miami and Charleston, so that each subset reproduces the site's design wind speed hazard curve and, at the same hazard level, the distributions of six other engineering quantities (two strong-wind duration measures, wind direction change, translation speed, distance to site, peak wind direction). The test is whether such subsets beat peak-speed-only selection on held-out quantities, giving the WRF and CFD lines a list of storms to simulate. The PI named it on 2026-10-26; before plan approval only literature work was done. Pre-set criteria (line assumptions) require, with 15 storms per site and at least two of three sites passing, design speed error of at most 3%, at least 80% of distribution cells consistent, held-out error of at most 10%, and an error at least one third lower than peak-only selection; if peak-only selection already passes, the result is recorded as "no increment", which is also a valid outcome. Seven precedent cards were checked: Danguri and Nishijima (2020) showed that three storms with the same peak speed gave steel damper fatigue of 1.9, 0.4 and 0.5 times that of the most likely storm, while the closest method, Du et al. (2023), clustered 16 of 160 records without weights, hazard-curve checks or comparison against peak-only selection.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project; start-up plan written (0 SU, at most 2 Colab compute units, about 9 person-days).
- **2026-10-26**: A quick literature search flagged Du et al. (2023); a clustering baseline and two criteria were added before any computation.
- **2026-10-26**: Four precedent cards checked against originals for two papers; none preserved peak, radius of maximum winds, duration and direction together.
- **2026-10-26**: Du et al. (2023) full text checked; the precedent gate concluded no overlap, so the novelty stands.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI's approval and a decision on per-site versus shared criteria (per-site recommended). The main risk is that the WRF line reconstructs historical typhoons, so a historical-storm variant was added and both user lines must confirm their needs after approval; Deep Research and a citation snowball come at the first milestone.

projects.title: L31.6j Stochastic Simulation and Multi-Fidelity Modeling of Peak Wind Pressure Distributions
projects.digest:
# Stochastic Emulation and Multi-Fidelity Prediction of Peak Wind Pressure Distributions (Not started)

L31.6j treats the peak pressure at a building tap as a random output rather than a fixed number: repeated wind tunnel tests or LES runs with a new seed give a different peak each time. The aim is to predict the whole peak distribution across wind directions, taps and building shapes with a stochastic emulator, and to fuse long wind tunnel records with short LES records in a multi-fidelity model. On 2026-10-26 the Lead agent wrote the start-up plan, which is awaiting the PI's approval. Under the approval gate, work so far is limited to literature search, reading existing material and writing the plan; no computation has been run. A citation snowball search (676 papers after de-duplication), a quick web search and three batches of literature cards found no study on the same question within the scope checked, but they narrowed the claimed novelty. Three independent reviewer models gave "support with reservations". The Lead agent accepted 8 must-fix items and revised the plan to v1.1.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The sub-project was opened as a branch of L31.6. The Lead agent drafted the plan. Pass criterion: on held-out wind directions and held-out shapes, mean CRPS at least 10% below a baseline of per-case Gumbel fits plus surrogate interpolation, with 90% interval coverage between 0.85 and 0.95. Planned cost: at most 1.0 Colab CPU compute unit, 0 supercomputer SU, about 6–8 person-days.
- **2026-10-26**: Deep Research returned HTTP 402 and was not done; a Gemini web search was used instead. A "20–30%" peak scatter figure from the topic note was dropped as unsupported.
- **2026-10-26**: Literature cards narrowed the novelty. Masters et al. 2010 already interpolated pressure distributions, and peak values directly, along eave height. Abdallah et al. 2019 already used input-dependent peak noise (12–24 seeds per case) in a multi-fidelity Kriging model for wind turbines. Diniz & Simiu 2005 give sampling CoVs of 0.09, 0.07 and 0.05 for 20, 30 and 60 min records. Takeuchi et al. 2026 split one LES run into 5 segments, so no citable figure exists for seed-to-seed LES peak scatter.
- **2026-10-26**: The precedent conclusion (plan v1.0) was sent to three reviewer models. All three gave "support with reservations".
- **2026-10-26**: The Lead agent adopted 8 must-fix items:
 - Models now predict and score only the distribution of a single block maximum, not the sampling error of a peak estimator.
 - Novelty is reduced to two points: cross-case prediction of the peak distribution with a coverage check, and wind tunnel–LES multi-fidelity. The near-term multi-fidelity test uses a proxy built from wind tunnel data only.
 - Missed neighbors were added, including Ke 2026 (mean pressure only) and Lamberti & Gorlé 2021 (nominal 95% intervals covering only 56–71%).
 - Decision terms were made exhaustive, and the scoring rules were defined in full.
 - Training and scoring blocks were separated by time halves.
 - 1-minute blocks (about 60 per case) were adopted.
 - The Duthinh 2018 numbers were corrected to a mean CoV of 5.94% rising to 13.24%, maximum 20.24%, as records shorten from 60 to 3 min.

## What the PI decided
- Liang Hu named this sub-project on 2026-10-26. Under the platform rules, naming a sub-project approves the topic but not the plan.

## Where it stands
Start-up plan v1.1 has been resubmitted and is waiting for the PI's approval. The parent project has decided that L31.6e and L31.6j will share one TPU low-rise dataset and one peak definition in the first stage; whether to merge with L31.6e and the division of work with L31.4 have been passed to the parent project.

projects.title: L31.6k Spatial Extremes and Multi-Station Joint Exceedance in Non-Typhoon Regions
projects.digest:
# L31.6k Spatial Extremes and Multi-Station Joint Exceedance in Non-Typhoon Regions (Not started)

This sub-project proposes to separate thunderstorm and synoptic winds in the US ASOS station network, fit spatial extreme-value models that can distinguish asymptotic dependence from asymptotic independence, and compute the probability that any one, or two or more, of N stations (or stations along a line) exceed their own 50-year gust in the same year, compared with an independence assumption; synthetic STORM typhoons would be treated the same way for a three-way comparison. The PI named it on 2026-10-26; before plan approval only literature work was done. The pre-set criterion for a visible bias from independence is a 90% interval lying wholly outside 0.67–1.5, a line convention without literature support. A quick search, a citation snowball (646 papers) and 12 new literature cards showed that Dawkins and Stephenson (2018) and others already studied spatial tail dependence and two-site joint exceedance for European storm gusts, mostly finding asymptotic independence, so the work is not a first. The remaining gap, within these 12 papers, is the US thunderstorm/synoptic split, design-level N-station exceedance against an independence baseline, and a typhoon comparison; the Lead agent describes this as an engineering increment, not a methods advance.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: The PI named the sub-project; start-up plan written (0 SU, at most 2 Colab compute units, about 8 person-days).
- **2026-10-26**: Second-stage Deep Research failed (quota unavailable) and is to be resent.
- **2026-10-26**: Literature cards checked; the expected result was changed to asymptotic independence and two parameters gained sources.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI's decisions on approval, region (recommended: central plains and Pacific Northwest), main return period (recommended: 50 years, with 700 years report-only) and whether to include Chinese stations (recommended: no).

projects.title: L31.6l Causal Damage Effects of Storm Duration and Repeated Impacts

# L31.6l Causal Effects of Storm Duration and Repeated Strikes on Damage (Exploring)

The sub-project, named by the PI on 2026-10-26, asks whether, at the same peak gust, longer strong-wind duration and repeated strikes in one season independently increase damage to low-rise buildings. The Lead agent's start-up plan makes step one a data scan (0 SU, Colab up to 0.5 CU, about 2 weeks) with three gates: at least 500 building-level records for one storm including undamaged houses and separating wind from water damage; enough duration contrast at similar peak wind; and power to detect an effect within 15% higher odds of damage escalation per extra hour. All thresholds are the Lead agent's own assumptions. After a quick precedent search, it read a 2014 insurance-claims regression finding duration a significant driver, but with losses allocated rather than observed, so the duration side is not a gap and the novelty narrows to building-level causal estimation. Repeated strikes remain unstudied quantitatively; a cited study turned out to concern an earthquake sequence.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-26**: Sub-project opened; start-up plan written and reported upward.
- **2026-10-26**: Quick precedent search returned (5 of 8 DOIs resolved); the plan was revised after checking originals.

## What the PI decided
- Named the sub-project; this counts as consent to open it, not plan approval.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI on approving step one, whether step two (Colab up to 2 CU) starts automatically if data pass, and whether to pursue non-public data later. No data downloaded and no computation run.

projects.title: L31.6m Risk Harmonization for Wind-Resistant Design in Mixed Climates
projects.digest:
# L31.6m Risk Harmonisation of Wind Design across Mixed Climates (Not started)

This sub-project asks how much the actual annual failure probability of building envelope components differs between typhoon-coast, transition and inland non-typhoon sites when all are designed to the same code format (ASCE 7-22, 700-year wind speed, factor 1.0), and whether an adjustment factor can bring site risks into rough agreement, ideally from a single rule based on the slope of the local hazard curve. The Chinese "50-year × 1.5" format would be applied only as a format comparison on the same US hazard curves. The PI named it on 2026-10-26; under the gate, only literature work and a start-up plan were done, with no computation. The plan estimates no supercomputer use, at most 0.5 Colab CPU compute units and about 2 weeks. The literature shows that load-level differences are known (Minciarelli 2001: load factor 2.14 on a Florida hurricane coast versus 1.55 in a non-hurricane region, checked against the original table), and that seismic studies find full risk matching impractical while harmonisation is achievable. The stated novelty is limited to component level, multi-site comparison and a harmonising factor, with a pre-set criterion that downgrades the work to a re-check if adding resistance scatter changes nothing.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-27**: Start-up plan written and reported, after a quick literature search and a 470-paper citation pool; Deep Research failed on a quota error.
- **2026-10-27**: The Lead agent proposed a division of work with L31.9a (code calibration) for the parent to confirm.
- **2026-10-27**: Seven precedent cards checked; one paper was found to cover only a single typhoon-region bridge, contrary to the quick search; a fastener resistance COV of 0.30 supports the 0.50 envelope scatter tier.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI's approval of the plan, of using the Chinese format only as a parallel comparison, and of deferring Chinese sites. The ASCE 2025 reliability chapter, the most likely overlapping precedent, is available only as an abstract and has been requested by interlibrary loan; it gates the first step and could shrink the work from about 8 to about 4 person-days or stop it.

projects.title: L31.6n Conformal Error Bands for AI Wind-Field and Wind-Pressure Surrogates
projects.digest:
# L31.6n Conformal Error Bands for AI Wind-Field and Wind-Pressure Surrogates (Not started)

This sub-project of L31.6, named by the PI on 10-26 under a plan-only gate, asks whether nominal 90% conformal prediction intervals for AI wind models keep their coverage on situations unseen in training (stronger typhoons, eyewall regions, critical pressure taps), and whether weighted, grouped, locally adaptive or quantile-regression variants can restore it. The Lead agent's startup plan fixes in advance that coverage below 0.80 counts as a breakdown and that a fix must bring coverage back to 0.85–0.95 without test labels and with interval width at most twice the original; cells with too few samples are reported but not judged. While writing the plan it found that a sister line (R25.3) had already applied conformal methods to wind-pressure surrogates, so pressure was proposed as a secondary line, and that no platform AI wind-field output has enough events, so the main line was proposed to use archived dropsonde profiles (116 storms, 7,524 profiles; 26 storms and 645 profiles with maximum wind of at least 60 m/s; 514 eyewall profiles). Literature checks found no prior conformal work on typhoon near-surface wind, boundary-layer profile or building-pressure surrogates. No model has been trained and nothing has been computed.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-27**: Startup plan submitted: at most 1.5 Colab CPU compute units, no supercomputer, about 2 weeks.
- **2026-10-27**: Citation snowball (4,120 records) screened by title by the Lead agent; 4 further neighbors found and sent for carding.
- **2026-10-27**: Two "unfound" DOIs in the quick-search report were shown to exist (trailing punctuation).
- **2026-10-27**: Four cards returned. The closest neighbor (pier scour, abstract only, not used as evidence) reports split-conformal coverage of 0.783 versus 0.898 for CQR in a shifted region at nominal 90%.
- **2026-10-27**: Ten full-text cards returned. The paper claiming coverage holds out of distribution recalibrates on data generated inside the new domain, so it does not test this question; the Lead agent corrected its earlier statement that the literature was contradictory.

## What the PI decided
- Named the sub-project; until the plan is approved only literature work, reading existing material and plan writing are allowed.

## Where it stands
Awaiting the PI on: approving the plan; the proposed rescoping (pressure as secondary line, main line on typhoon wind-field and profile surrogates); and what to do if a data probe shows too few samples, which the Lead agent suggests deciding later.

# L31.8 风机抗台风韧性与性能化设计

编号：L31.8 · 状态：在做（Liang Hu 10-21 批准启动方案；平台 10-21 登记 A183 开闸）

## 目标
把"风机的性能化/韧性设计"拆成四层可检验的设计问题（结构、卸载系统、失效顺序、经济与韧性，含冲刷等多灾种），判断现有工作做到了哪一层；第一步量化台风极端风下"卸载失效"与"提高风级"两个杠杆的大小，为性能目标该围绕什么来定提供依据。

## 来源（Liang Hu 原话，10-21 L29）
1. 「风机台风下破坏就比较常见了，这里面有很多问题。风机的基于性能（韧性）的设计现在是不是一个全新的课题？」
2. 「风机的抗风设计还必须考虑经济性和发电效率的平衡，还有冲刷等荷载的影响，也是个典型的风荷载主导的多灾害韧性和性能设计的问题」
3. 「这个进入核心实验室」
5. （10-22）「我感觉文献数量还很不充分，特别是在执行计算前，你很多都没有仔细查。……风机还有一个独特的点，是它是动态的，是一边运行一边调控。……这个问题牵连非常广大，恐怕下面各个component都要查文献。」
4. （10-21 批复）「这是一个核心课题，我批准你现在的初步方案。需要注意一点，这个实际上是对整个performance、resilience用于风力机，因此是全概率积分链条上各个环节的全面提升加上风机部分的实际考虑，后续还需要参考L29.3的相关内容。风机的验证材料较多，这是个优势。」

## 当前状态
10-25：按 Liang Hu 六问分拆为 L31.8a–f 六个子项目，各自做文献轮并交启动方案（10-29 前）；决策。
10-22：**计算暂停，先按部件补文献**（Liang Hu 10-22：执行计算前文献不充分；风机是动态的，一边运行一边调控）。M2 批作业 CRC 1603230 302/336 正常、34 例致命中止（S2 偏航 30° 全失败；57 m/s 下 S1 偏航 30°/60° 各 5 例），不归约、不判读，待 C3 文献判断是物理失稳还是模型越界。10-22 R 部件 6 张卡回来后：失败的 30° 偏航与已报道的停机失速诱发失稳一致（Wang 2017、Höning 2026），但我们的极曲线（带旋转修正）、UA_Mod=3、ElastoDyn 小角度叶片和零转速 BEMT 都是文献点名的敏感项。物理与模型越界仍分不开。另外 302 个正常例子里有 91 例越出 ElastoDyn 小角度假设，须先筛选才能用；判别实验只写设计、不提交（ 末节）。5 份快查已回（线索在）；Deep Research：C 环（运行与控制）一份已完成，10-22 核对后只当线索用，有 2 处张冠李戴，ROSCO 的 `Vstorm` 参数不存在，见；R、H 两份因额度 90/90 用尽未做。10-22 C/H/D/L 四环 18 张卡已回（7 篇全文）；10-22 晚：Liang Hu 解除文献暂停，按 查本地——待取清单中 12 篇本地早有（9 篇有 PDF，交 litwiki 建卡；3 篇 Zotero 有条目无附件），其余 36 篇交 literature 取件（Elsevier 走）；规范仍待 ND 图书馆。第四批 12 篇 OA 原文卡已建。旋转失速修正不适用于锁定转子已有文献依据（Loubeyres 2022 PDF p.5｜文章页 4）。付费缺口 25 项列在；改跑 五环（池 109–475 条），人工初筛 73 篇交 litwiki 建卡；11-02 前交分部件文献综述 v1。状态报告。

# L31.8 Wind Turbine Typhoon Resilience and Performance-Based Design

## Objective
Decompose "performance-based/resilient design of wind turbines" into four testable design tiers (structure, load-shedding system, failure sequence, and economics/resilience, including multi-hazards such as scour), and determine which tier existing work has reached; as a first step, quantify the relative magnitude of two levers under extreme typhoon winds, "load-shedding failure" vs "upgrading wind class", to provide a basis for what performance targets should center on.

## Current Status
10-25: Split into six subprojects L31.8a-f per Liang Hu's six questions, each conducting a literature round and submitting a launch plan (before 10-29); decision .
10-22: **Computation paused, supplementing literature by component first** (Liang Hu 10-22: literature is insufficient prior to running computations; a wind turbine is dynamic, regulating while operating). M2 batch job had 302/336 normal runs and 34 fatal aborts (all S2 30° yaw cases failed; 5 cases each for S1 30°/60° yaw at 57 m/s); no reduction or interpretation performed, awaiting C3 literature to determine whether this is physical instability or model out-of-bounds. 10-22 after 6 cards for component R returned: the failed 30° yaw cases are consistent with reported parked stall-induced instability (Wang 2017, Höning 2026), but our polars (with rotational correction), UA_Mod=3, ElastoDyn small-angle blade assumption, and zero-speed BEMT are all sensitive items flagged in the literature. Physical instability and model out-of-bounds remain inseparable. Furthermore, 91 of the 302 normal runs exceed the ElastoDyn small-angle assumption and must be filtered before use; discriminative experiments are designed on paper only and not submitted (final section of). 5 quick searches returned (leads in); Deep Research: one report for ring C (operation and control) completed, used only as leads after 10-22 verification due to 2 misattributions, and ROSCO's `Vstorm` parameter does not exist, see; reports for rings R and H were not run as the 90/90 quota was exhausted. 10-22 18 cards across rings C/H/D/L returned (7 full texts); 10-22 evening: Liang Hu lifted the literature pause, checked local holdings per : 12 papers on the retrieval list were already held locally (9 with PDFs, sent to litwiki for card creation; 3 with Zotero entries but no attachments), remaining 36 sent to literature for retrieval (Elsevier via); standards still awaiting ND library. Batch 4 of 12 OA full-text cards created. Literature basis found confirming rotational stall correction does not apply to a locked rotor (Loubeyres 2022 PDF p.5 | article p.4). 25 paywalled gaps listed in; switched to running five rings (pool of 109-475 entries), manually pre-screened 73 papers sent to litwiki for card creation; component-wise literature review v1 due before 11-02. Status report .

## Decisions Made
- 10-25 Intelligence E2 (Tariq et al. arXiv 2607.16962, multi-directional TMDI in OpenFAST StC, IEA 15 MW wind-wave case, abstract level): from L31.8's perspective, judged X1 for archiving without a separate card (primary evaluation by L30.2). Kept as a structural-control backup for M3 control strategies: it controls tower-top normal operating wind-wave response, whereas L31.8 focuses on blade stall-induced edgewise vibration under typhoon parked/idling conditions, so the two cannot substitute for each other; if L30.2 close reading confirms open code, M3 can directly reuse its StC implementation for tower damping comparison.
- 10-22 Paused computation, supplementing component-wise literature first; ring C changed to dynamic control process → 
- 10-21 Launch plan approved, framework changed to ring-by-ring enhancement along the full probabilistic integral chain →

# L31.8a Wind Turbine Typhoon Failure Modes and a Validation Database (Not started)

This sub-project of L31.8 (multi-hazard typhoon resilience and performance-based design of wind turbines) responds to the PI's question of how fragility, resilience and performance analysis could enter design, which requires accurate modeling of every link, especially failure modes, and a database to validate them. It asks three things: a complete list of turbine typhoon failure modes with the accuracy and validation status of existing models; which public turbine failure cases and post-typhoon surveys exist and what fields they contain; and whether a validation database can be built and what minimum data it needs. Under a plan-only gate, the Lead agent did literature work only. Its v0 conclusion (not reviewed) is that typhoon accidents can test parts of the probabilistic chain, but public records are insufficient and the key "response to failure" link cannot yet be tested. Of 12 typhoon or hurricane events scored on 12 validation fields, field coverage was 62% including inferred values and 32% first-hand; none had both nacelle wind measurement and per-turbine control-state records, and none had consequence data. Version 1 of the failure-mode list, based on 27 full-text cards, found that failure-stage model errors against tests or accidents are reported in only 3 of 27 papers.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-25**: Division of work agreed with L29.1d: per-turbine accident cases are kept only in the L29.1d case library; L31.8a defines validation-grade fields and assesses coverage.
- **2026-10-25**: A web search on model accuracy was checked against originals; a tower-buckling round robin (21%–30% scatter in nonlinear analysis of the same 8 MW tower) was confirmed, while several accident failure chains in the report were wrong and rejected.
- **2026-10-25**: Startup plan submitted: 9 failure-mode classes, a draft field specification and data requirements for owners and regulators, including a wind-field reconstruction accuracy of about ±5% that the Lead agent derived itself and flagged for review.
- **2026-10-25**: Of 31 papers requested, 24 full texts were obtained; first-hand Chinese accident surveys were essentially unavailable from public sources.
- **2026-10-25**: Failure-mode list v1: e.g. a 3.7% gap between design curve and lowest cylinder test (not a whole tower); in one floating-turbine comparison, mean model underestimates of about 10% to 20% in wave-only cases; yaw and pitch holding devices have no mechanical model or validation. Error figures from the quick search were not found in the originals and were dropped.

## What the PI decided
- Asked how fragility and performance analysis could enter design, calling for accurate failure-mode modeling and a validation database built from turbine failure cases and post-typhoon surveys.
- Ruled earlier that MDPI papers are not to be fetched.

## Where it stands
The plan awaits the PI's approval (2 weeks, no supercomputer). The PI is also asked whether to request typhoon-period SCADA and per-turbine damage records from owners, manufacturers or regulators; the Lead agent suggests deciding after the conclusion draft with its data-requirement list.
